name: The Dr Harmon household
head: harmon_elijah_d

arrival.note: 'He arrived at Chicago in May, 1830; his family following him the succeeding year.' Month precision, and the family's arrival a year behind him is stated separately.

party_size_on_arrival.note: He came alone and his family followed in 1831 - the source distinguishes the two journeys, which almost none of them do.

origin.note: He practised at Burlington from 1806 and brought his medicines 'from the Green Mountains'.

reason_for_coming.value: Financial reverses and an attempt to recover in the West
reason_for_coming.note: 'In 1829 the Doctor suffered some pecuniary reverses and resolved to attempt recuperation in the Great West.' THE PLAINEST STATEMENT OF MOTIVE IN THE PARCEL, and one that is not gold-rush optimism but debt.

lives_at.note: 'His residence was a cabin of hewn logs' now has a structure to point at. The household's presence on the scene date remains uncertain and the link does not change that. Linked by the inferred-household programme's building parcel (docs/ROADMAP.md K1, phase two); the building record carries the evidence.

works_at.note: He was post surgeon at the fort in 1830-32 and in private practice besides; by the scene date he was neither, on his own record. No link is made.

last_dated_appearance.note: NO SIGHTING, SO THE LEG IS A SOURCE'S SPAN. The card holds no dated reading of this person at or before the scene date; the date here is the far end of what a cited source COVERS, which the role's own note calls the source's bound and not the man's. Read from `roles[] (source_span)` as `1673/1857`, which reaches 1857-12-31 — a window that covers 1835-07-01 itself, so it pins no last sighting before the day and cannot be read as one. THE FIELD IS THE EVIDENCE UNDER THE VERDICT, not a new claim: nothing here moves the presence off `uncertain`, and T-1159 and T-1172 classify this household by this date instead of reading it out of the prose (T-1144 acceptance 9).

present_on_scene_date.note: THE ONE HOUSEHOLD IN THIS PARCEL WHOSE HEAD IS DOCUMENTED TO HAVE LEFT. Andreas: 'In 1834, Dr. Harmon migrated to Texas, and until the time of his death - January 3, 1869 - divided his sojourns between that State and Chicago.' A man who divides his sojourns between Texas and Chicago is in one of them on 1 July 1835 and the source does not say which. Recorded as uncertain, and it must not be silently resolved to 'present' because his sons were here.

persons.name: Dr Elijah Dewey Harmon

occupation.note: 'The Father of Medicine in Chicago' in Andreas's phrase. He arrived in May 1830, took the place of the absent Dr Finley as post surgeon at Fort Dearborn, isolated and treated the cholera cases of July 1832 and quarrelled with General Scott over it, and in the winter of 1832 performed 'the first surgical operation of any importance' in Chicago - an amputation on a half-breed Canadian who had frozen his feet carrying the mail on horseback from Green Bay.

persons.note: HIS STOCK IN TRADE IS DESCRIBED AND IT IS THE MOST CONCRETE MATERIAL DETAIL ABOUT ANY PERSON IN THIS PARCEL: 'A case of rusty instruments, a library of about one hundred volumes and a stock of medicines brought from the Green Mountains ... His residence was a cabin of hewn logs; his larder, a repository of flour, bacon and coffee.' Born at Bennington, Vermont, 20 August 1782; married Welthyan Loomis 30 October 1808; volunteer surgeon aboard the Saratoga at Plattsburg in 1814. He pre-empted one hundred and forty acres whose northern boundary was near Sixteenth Street. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 2 times, as “HARMON ELIJAH D”, 1834-10-02: 1 federal land entry — SWFR sec 22 T39N R14E, 276.48 acres stated in all, for $345.60 (ls0435, ls0436). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS COOK, UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. The register states this purchaser's residence as COOK, so the sale is contemporary evidence that a man of this name lived in Cook County on the date of sale. It is not evidence that he lived in the town. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: HARMON ELIJAH D matches Dr Elijah Dewey Harmon: the forename names Dr Elijah Dewey Harmon of the 6 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Harmon, Mrs. E. C. | Letter. | November 29, 1882.” (second_presb_0181, printed page 164), admitted 1882-11-29 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Harmon' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins E. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” THE LINE IS A MARRIED WOMAN'S ENTRY, and the crosswalk's own Mrs rule governs what it can have met: “a line flagged a_married_womans_entry that meets a MAN in the 1835 layer has met his name, not him: it corroborates that the name was a Chicago name in the 1840s and it does not put that man on this roll.” The match is filed rather than suppressed, because a suppressed match is invisible and a flagged one can be argued with. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

resident_research.summary: Corroborated in a volume printed after the scene date. Dr Elijah Dewey Harmon agrees with an entry in the Fergus 1839/1843 and Norris 1844 directories. The reading enriches the biography and adds no 1835 attestation.
resident_research.notes: FERGUS 26-29, AS PRINTED: "Harmon, Eli[j]ah D[e]we[y], physician, bds C. L. Harmon [died January 3, 1869, aged 80]". The 1843 directory prints the full given names Elijah Dewey behind this project's 'Dr Elijah Dewey Harmon', with the same trade the 1835 record carries, and a death date and age that put birth about 1788-89. Research only. Later-volume readings are recorded here and NOT promoted: T-0513 consolidates and T-0514/T-0515 apply.

roles.note: THE BOUND IS THE SOURCE'S, NOT THE MAN'S. This role is carried by the card's 1835 occupation block and is dated by what the cited source or sources are ABOUT, which is why `precision` can be no better than the span they cover. The span reaches 1835, so this role stands in the scene-date view. The printing the trade was read off is not on the card and is fetched by T-1254.

A TRADE PRINTED IN THE 1843 DIRECTORY, 8 years after the scene, carried here by its crosswalk (T-1254, by tools/derive_resident_roles.py). It is NOT a claim about 1835-07-01 and never becomes one: back-projecting a later volume onto the scene is the defect T-1145 exists to refuse. `place` is the address or place of business the record states in its own column; a firm named only inside the printed line stays in `as_printed` for the business band to rule on.

persons.name: The Harmon daughter later known as Mrs A. G. Burley

occupation.note: No source records an occupation for this person. This is the ABSENCE of a record rather than a claim that they did no work - the sources of 1835 name the occupations of household heads and almost never those of wives, children or the people counted with them.

persons.note: NAMED BY THE SOURCE AS A RELATIVE, NOT AS A RESIDENT. Andreas's particulars of Dr Elijah Dewey Harmon come from 'his daughter Mrs A. G. Burley', writing or speaking about fifty years after the scene date. WHAT THIS RECORD IS: a daughter the source names, seated in her father's household because that is the household this layer holds for her. WHAT IT IS NOT: her name in 1835. 'Mrs A. G. Burley' is a married style built on a husband's initials and the marriage is later than the scene; her own forename is printed nowhere this project has read. No birth year is claimed, so no age follows: the marriage of 30 October 1808 bounds her birth after it and nothing bounds it before 1835. The household's presence stands at 'uncertain' and she inherits it.

age_band.note: NO BAND IS DRAWN, AND THE REASON IS THIS CARD'S OWN. A household seats this person as its child and the same record names them in a married style, printed by a source later than the scene. A KINSHIP WORD IS NOT AN AGE (T-1179) and a married style is not one either: neither is dated to 1 July 1835, and they cannot both be read as a band. None of this pass's three conditionings fits, and a band drawn from the schedule's child columns would make a married woman a child under fifteen. This row names ONE person, which is why it does not carry the collective refusal it used to: the refusal is T-1395's and the reason is the card's.

persons.note: NAMED AND DATED IN THE SOURCE - Andreas's biography of Dr Elijah Dewey Harmon gives the marriage as 'married Welthyan Loomis 30 October 1808', twenty-seven years before the scene date. WHAT THE SOURCE DOES NOT SAY: it does not say she came west with him, and nothing in this project places her at Chicago on 1 July 1835. She is written because a named wife of a named head is the person this layer exists to record, and the presence on the day is the reconstruction, not the marriage. The household's own present_on_scene_date stands at 'uncertain' for the doctor - Andreas has him leaving for the lead mines - and she inherits that doubt exactly. No age, no occupation and no arrival is claimed for her.

basis.note: Drawn from the 1840 Chicago schedule's column 'free white females 30 under 40', one of its female bands, conditioned on `named_on_a_roll_15_and_over` because the person is named in their own right on any other roll this layer was minted from - a letter list, a subscription, a court docket, a trade notice - or carries a role, a trade, a marriage or a parenthood.

age_band.note: AN AGE BAND, NEVER A YEAR. No source this project holds bears on when this person was born, so the band is drawn from the only committed sex by age distribution the project has - the 1840 Chicago schedule, five years after the scene and a town twice the size - seeded by this person's own id ('harmon_welthyan:age_bands_1840'). AND THE CONDITIONING IS THE MODEL'S, NOT A SOURCE'S: that a roll naming a person in their own right names somebody 15 or over. The 1840 schedule counts a child as a tally inside a household and never as a correspondent; 15 rather than 20 because an apprentice or a journeyman stands on a trade roll. No source states this rule. No exact year is written, because a year drawn from a decadal band would read as a record of a birth.

research_note: A DOCUMENTED RESIDENT WHO MAY HAVE BEEN IN TEXAS, kept in the dataset precisely because the presence field can say so. Dropping him would lose the town's first doctor, his hewn-log cabin, his hundred books and the only stated economic motive in the parcel; asserting him would be a claim the source contradicts. HIS FAMILY IS THE REASON THE HOUSEHOLD MATTERS ANYWAY: the Harmon brothers' dry-goods firm is a separate household here, Harmon Court is named for him, and his daughter Mrs A. G. Burley supplied Andreas with these particulars fifty years later - which is a useful reminder that a good deal of what looks like documentation in this book is family recollection with a name attached.

kin.note: FATHER OF THE HARMON BROTHERS. Andreas's life of the doctor lists his five surviving children, and that sentence is what resolved the newspaper masthead 'C. & I. Harmon' into his two eldest sons — it is the reason this household exists at all. Graded inferred: the parentage is stated, the identification of the initials with these cards is this project's. Ruled under T-0734; found by PR #947.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. WHAT THIS PASS RULED ONTO THIS HOUSEHOLD, named so the ruling can be found again: each volume below is followed by the printed entries it set against this person and the status the crosswalk ruled them at — a single entry carries what its own `could_carry` declares, and an ambiguous or contested match carries nothing and is shown so that the silence is legible. harmon_elijah_d, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 — f1839_e0640 (a single entry); harmon_elijah_d, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 — f1843_e1208 (a single entry).
